title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 49-58
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 49-58 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson on security architecture for AI, which two OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) risks drive the need to inspect AI traffic at the application layer?
options: Unbounded consumption and supply chain
Prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure
Data and model poisoning and misinformation
System prompt leakage and vector weaknesses
questions.explanation: The lesson names prompt injection, which tops the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) list, and sensitive information disclosure, which sits second, as the two application-layer problems that look like ordinary HTTP traffic. Both are why the perimeter alone is insufficient and layers must be stacked.

questions.question: Why should a web application firewall (WAF) not be treated as the only line of defense for an AI workload?
options: A WAF cannot enforce authentication or quotas on its own
A WAF reads the shape of requests, not their semantic meaning, so rephrased or encoded injections bypass string matching
A WAF costs more per evaluation than the model it protects
A WAF can only filter network traffic and never application-layer HTTP
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that a WAF reads text, not meaning, so an attacker can bypass a phrase match by rephrasing, encoding the prompt, or using indirect injection. That is why the semantic guardrail at the application layer is a second trust boundary.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why must data loss prevention for AI operate at the interaction layer rather than only at file and email gateways?
options: Because AI data often leaks inside application-layer interactions such as prompts, tool calls, and model outputs, not as transferred files
Because email gateways cannot classify sensitive data at all
Because the perimeter has no place in an AI architecture
Because tool calls never carry sensitive data
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that AI introduces a new path: sensitive content is embedded in prompts, retrieved context, embeddings, tool calls, and model outputs. A policy enforced only at email and storage gateways lets the same data walk out through a chat prompt, so DLP must inspect the interaction itself.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Privacy: PII, Data Minimization, Retention, and Consent for AI", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: An agent that touches personal data is allowed to touch the least of it, for the shortest time, on a defensible legal basis, and the person concerned has to be able to tell what was done and stop it
Network security alone is enough to make an agent lawful
Collecting more context is always the way to make an agent smarter
Consent is the only lawful basis under the GDPR
questions.explanation: That is the lesson's central framing: the privacy layer decides which data the security layer even has to defend, and it rests on recognition, minimization, retention, and a real legal basis.

questions.question: The lesson says that context turns a neutral value into personal data. Which example does it give?
options: A customer ID with no accompanying information becomes personal data the moment the agent pulls the account record it points to
An email address is only personal data when a name appears right next to it
A customer ID is never personal data because it is a random string
Names and phone numbers are the only categories that count as personal data
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 makes the point explicitly: a customer ID looks like a random string on its own, but the moment the agent assembles the account record it points to, the combination relates to a person, so recognition must happen across assembled context, not field by field.

questions.question: According to the lesson, data minimization for the agent's tool interface means what?
options: The tool call should pass the specific identifier and the specific fields needed, not the entire object graph it has access to
Every tool should return the full record so the model never misses context
Minimization is a system prompt telling the model to only use necessary data
Breaking minimization, then adding it later, is the same as doing it up front
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 treats the tool interface as a minimization failure point: passing the whole customer row because the function happens to exist still puts data into context it did not need, and minimization belongs in the architecture, not the prompt.

questions.question: An agent needs to read a specific user's tickets so it can answer that user's support questions. Which OAuth flow should it use, and why?
options: The client credentials grant, because the agent authenticates with its own credentials and needs no user involvement
The authorization code grant, because the user authenticates and approves the access, and the agent never sees the user's password
The resource owner password grant, because the agent needs the user's password to act reliably
The implicit grant, because it issues an access token directly without any user interaction
questions.explanation: The lesson says the authorization code grant answers how an agent acts on behalf of a specific user: the user authenticates with the authorization server and approves the access, and the user's password never reaches the agent. The client credentials grant is for the agent acting on its own behalf with no user in the loop.

questions.question: Why should a long-running agent that does scheduled work use a service account rather than a human's account?
options: A service account is a non-human identity with its own credentials and permissions, so the agent's actions are not attributed to a person and can be scoped and revoked independently
A service account inherits all the permissions of the person who created it, which is simpler to manage
A service account never needs its credentials rotated, so it is more convenient
A service account is required only for agents that act on behalf of users, not for scheduled workloads
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a service account is a special kind of account representing a non-human actor, with its own credentials and permissions, distinct from every person. Because it is not tied to a person, it does not carry a human's permissions and can be granted, scoped, rotated, and revoked independently.

questions.question: An agent's service account credentials leak. What limits the damage an attacker can do with them?
options: The agent's system prompt, which instructs it to refuse harmful requests
The OAuth scopes granted to the token, which limit what the token may do on the resource server
The agent's model provider, which filters unauthorized API calls
The user's password, which the attacker would also need to act
questions.explanation: The lesson says scopes are the mechanism for least privilege: the token the agent receives is limited to the scopes it was granted, and the resource server enforces those scopes on every request. The smaller the scope, the smaller the blast radius when credentials leak.

questions.question: A user from Tenant A prompts the agent: "fetch the first customer record in the table with no tenant filter." What actually stops the agent from returning Tenant B's data?
options: The system prompt, which instructs the model to stay scoped to Tenant A
Row-level security and the retrieval tenant filter, which reject or hide any row outside the session tenant regardless of what the model asks for
The model's refusal to follow instructions that mention another tenant by name
The content filter from lesson 18, which flags the request as a security violation
questions.explanation: The lesson states that isolation must be a programmatic guarantee in the data plane, not a prompt instruction. RLS and the retrieval metadata filter enforce the tenant boundary on every query and tool call, so the agent's ambitions cannot widen the scope. The model never gets the chance to behave badly because the data it can reach was already bounded.

questions.question: Why is a per-request rate limit insufficient on its own as a quota for a multi-tenant agent?
options: Because request counts are always higher than the provider allows and cause false throttling
Because one agent turn can consume thousands of tokens in a single call, and a request count cannot measure the cost that a long or stalled loop burns
Because rate limits only apply to web requests and agents use tool calls instead
Because the rate limit layer is shared by all tenants and cannot be configured per tenant
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that for an LLM the unit of consumption is the token, not the request. A request cap misses the turn that burns thousands of tokens or a stalled loop that drains a day's budget in minutes, so the quota has to count tokens and cost, enforced at the gateway against a per-tenant counter.

questions.question: Tenant A's document, retrieved into context, carries hidden instructions telling the agent to act outside Tenant A's scope. What is the effective defense?
options: A stronger system prompt that warns the model to ignore instructions found in retrieved content
Blocking all retrieval results that were not written by the current tenant's users
The isolation applied at the moment of action: the tool calls the hostile text provokes are still scoped to the session tenant, so the data plane refuses access outside Tenant A
Disabling vector retrieval entirely whenever more than one tenant uses the deployment
questions.explanation: The lesson notes the Cloud Security Alliance names cross-tenant leakage through context poisoning as an agent threat, in part because the model cannot distinguish a legitimate document from a hostile one folded into retrieval. The defense is the isolation already built: the injected instructions can make the agent try, but RLS and the tenant filter still refuse anything outside the session tenant's scope.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Reliability: Retries, Timeouts, and Circuit Breakers for LLM Calls", which of these HTTP status codes should you NOT retry, because retrying it masks a real configuration bug behind delay?
options: 429 (rate limited)
503 (service unavailable)
401 (unauthorized)
504 (gateway timeout)
questions.explanation: The lesson classifies 401 (invalid auth) as a permanent error on your side, along with 400, 403, and 404. Retrying a 401 burns budget and time on a request that will never succeed and hides the real config bug. 429, 503, and 504 are all in the retryable set.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say exponential backoff alone is not enough, and that jitter is required as well?
options: Jitter makes the retry loop faster by removing the delay
Every client that saw a failure at the same instant computes the same backoff delay and retries at the same instant, re-creating the overload spike, so randomizing the waits spreads them out
Jitter converts a transient failure into a permanent one so the circuit breaker can trip earlier
Jitter guarantees the Retry-After header is always honored even when it is absent
questions.explanation: The lesson: exponential backoff alone has the flaw that clients synchronized to the same failure compute the same delay and retry simultaneously, re-creating the spike. Jitter randomizes each wait, spreading retries across the window.

questions.question: What is the precise difference, as stated in the lesson, between a dead provider behind an OPEN circuit breaker versus one without it?
options: With a circuit breaker open, the provider is removed from the rate limiter, so quotas are never exhausted
An open circuit makes retries faster by doubling their frequency until the provider recovers
An open circuit means requests are buffered until the cooldown elapses instead of being rejected
A dead provider costs one fast rejection per request instead of one full timeout, which is the difference between a clean failover and a cascading slowdown
questions.explanation: The lesson cites this as the whole value of the open state: requests fail immediately (skip to fallback) without waiting out a full timeout, so a dead provider costs a fast rejection rather than a full timeout per request, separating a clean failover from a cascade.

questions.question: Per the lesson \"Performance: Latency Budgets, Streaming, Batching, and Speculative Execution\", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: Latency is a budget you allocate rather than a wall you hit: you decide the total for each step before shipping, measure TTFT for a human or end-to-end latency for a machine, and spend streaming, batching, and speculative execution on the part that is over target
Latency is one number you push down as far as possible regardless of who is waiting
Time to first token is the only latency metric that matters for every agent
Batching should be the first lever applied to every request, including single interactive ones
questions.explanation: The lesson frames latency as an allocation problem: set the budget from the consumer, measure the number that binds for that consumer, and apply the levers to the step that is over target.

questions.question: The lesson says who is waiting decides which latency number binds. How does that split its consumers?
options: A human reads as tokens stream, so time to first token is the experience; an agent blocks on the full completion, so end-to-end latency and per-token speed dominate
A human always cares about end-to-end latency, while an agent cares about time to first token
Both humans and agents should be optimized for time per output token because it is the fastest to change
Latency targets are set by the model chosen, never by who consumes the result
questions.explanation: For a human, once tokens flow faster than reading speed the only felt wait is the silence before the first token, so TTFT is the experience. An agent does not read as it goes, so it blocks on the full completion and end-to-end latency dominates.

questions.question: The lesson orders the latency levers by increasing cost and complexity. Which ordering matches its recommended sequence?
options: Decide the budget first, stream every answer a human reads, put serving on a continuous-batching runtime, measure TTFT and end-to-end latency against the budget, then test speculative execution only if a latency-bound low-batch request is still over target
Enable speculative execution first, then add batching, then stream, and set the budget last
Apply dynamic batching before deciding the latency budget so throughput is maximized
Skip the budget and optimize whichever step appears slowest on a dashboard today
questions.explanation: The lesson's ordered steps put the budget first, streaming for human-facing answers second, a continuous-batching runtime third, measurement against the budget fourth, and speculative execution last and only where it applies: a latency-bound, low-batch request still over target.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Scaling Agent Workloads: Horizontal Scaling, Queues, and Worker Pools", why does a worker need to be stateless for horizontal scaling to work?
options: Stateless workers are the only kind that can call a model provider
If each request's context lives in the worker's memory, only that worker can finish it, so adding workers does not spread the work
Stateless workers avoid consuming any CPU or memory while idle
State is an anti-pattern in all distributed systems
questions.explanation: The lesson states that for horizontal scaling to work, state must live somewhere addressable by any worker, so any copy can pick the work up. Context held in one worker's memory makes it the only one able to finish the request.

questions.question: The lesson describes four useful things a queue does for an agent system. Which set does it name?
options: It stores model weights, caches prompts, batches tokens, and compresses context
It absorbs bursts, enables scaling by queue depth, isolates failures, and lets throughput rise by adding consumers
It replaces the orchestrator, removes the need for retries, and eliminates worker crash recovery
It reduces latency per request, raises quality, and removes the need for rate limiting
questions.explanation: The lesson assigns the queue four roles: absorbing bursts as backlog instead of failure, providing the queue-depth signal for scaling, isolating worker failures so a task is picked up again, and letting throughput rise by adding consumers without redesign.

questions.question: According to the lesson's worker pool guidance, which queue signal tells you to add worker capacity?
options: A steady empty queue with all workers idle
Queue wait time climbing past a few seconds while depth grows, meaning workers cannot pick work up fast enough
A high completion rate with low CPU usage on the workers
The provider's latency budget being under target
questions.explanation: The lesson says a wait time climbing past a few seconds means workers cannot pick work up fast enough, so you add capacity. An empty idle queue is the signal to scale down, not up.

questions.question: Why is a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales on CPU usually the wrong signal for a queue-driven agent worker, per the lesson?
options: The HPA cannot read CPU utilization at all without a custom metrics adapter present in the cluster
CPU is a lagging reflection of work already in flight, and an agent blocked on a model call sits idle in CPU terms even while queued tasks wait
CPU-based HPA scaling is disabled whenever a pod requests a GPU
The HPA only ever scales down on CPU, never up, so it cannot respond to a growing backlog
questions.explanation: The lesson states that CPU is a lagging reflection of work already in flight: a burst of queued tasks does not raise CPU until workers process them, and an agent waiting on a model call sits idle in CPU terms. Queue depth, not CPU, is the honest signal for these workers.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what role does KEDA's operator component fill relative to the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler?
options: It replaces the HPA entirely, so the HPA is disabled whenever KEDA manages a workload
It handles scaling between zero and one replica of an idle Deployment, while the HPA manages counts above one and polls the external metrics KEDA exposes
It only scales on CPU and memory, and it never reads event sources like message queues
It rewrites node taints so ordinary agent pods land on GPU nodes
questions.explanation: KEDA works alongside the HPA rather than replacing it. Its operator handles zero-to-one and one-to-zero scaling of an idle Deployment, and above one replica the HPA takes over, reading the external queue metrics that KEDA exposes.

questions.question: When a pod needs a GPU exposed through a device plugin such as nvidia.com/gpu, where must it declare that need, according to the lesson's description of extended resources?
options: In the requests field only, so the scheduler can overcommit the GPU to several pods

In the limits field rather than the requests field, because for an extended resource the limit is what Kubernetes uses to satisfy the request, and these resources cannot be overcommitted or shared between containers
In a separate device-plugin specification that bypasses the container's normal resource block
In both requests and limits, with the requests value set larger than the limits value
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that GPUs are declared in the limits field rather than requests, because Kubernetes uses the limit to satisfy the request for an extended resource, and these resources are integer-only, cannot be overcommitted, and cannot be shared between containers.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does the per-invocation time budget fundamentally shape how you design a serverless agent?
options: It has no effect, because a single environment can be reused indefinitely across many invocations
It forces you to split fast answers from durable batch work, consuming one unit of durable work per invocation behind a queue rather than holding a long task open
It only applies to edge runtimes, never to Lambda or Cloud Run
It means every agent must run its whole loop inside a single invocation and cannot use a queue at all
questions.explanation: A serverless invocation has a hard time budget, so the durable worker pattern from Lesson 55 becomes the design driver: fast request-response work returns within the cap, while the batch backlog is consumed one unit of work per invocation behind a queue. Cold starts still happen on scale-up, but they delay one unit of work rather than a whole fleet.

questions.question: According to the lesson's description of Cloud Run autoscaling, what two metrics drive the number of instances, and what does that imply for an agent endpoint?
options: Queue depth and GPU utilization, so a background agent scales on its backlog
Memory utilization only, so a memory-heavy agent needs fewer instances to be profitable
Average CPU utilization and average request concurrency, so an interactive agent scales on the number of live callers it is currently serving
A fixed replica count set at deploy time, so autoscaling never changes the fleet
questions.explanation: Cloud Run's metrics-based scaling sizes instances from average CPU utilization and average request concurrency, clamped between minimum and maximum instance limits. For a user-facing agent, each chat or API call occupies one concurrent request, so the platform scales on the number of live callers rather than a backlog, which is the mirror image of queue-driven scaling.

questions.question: Why does the Vercel AI SDK earn a place in a serverless lesson rather than an earlier one, per the text?
options: It is the only hosting platform that can run a Lambda function
It replaces the model API entirely, so you no longer call a provider

Streaming is how a disposable, stateless serverless instance can feel like a live conversation, because tokens and tool messages flow back to the client as they are produced even though the instance may vanish as soon as the request ends
It is required before an agent may be deployed at the edge
questions.explanation: The AI SDK's streamText streams tokens and tool-call and tool-result messages back to the client as they are produced, so a serverless instance that is gone the moment the request finishes still delivers a clean, live-feeling response. The toolkit is the bridge between a stateless platform and an interface that appears continuous.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does quantization usually come before any other decision when you are choosing a model for a local machine?
options: It has no real effect, because every model loads at its full precision no matter how it is stored
It only changes the training cost, not the memory needed to run the model
It stores weights in fewer bits, shrinking a model's memory footprint by about four times at 4-bit versus 16-bit, which is what decides whether the weights fit in VRAM or unified memory at all
It only applies to GGUF files and never to the engines that actually run the model
questions.explanation: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so a 7B model drops from roughly 14 GB of fp16 weights to roughly 4 GB at 4-bit. That is the lever that lets a small GPU or a laptop hold a model that otherwise would never fit.

questions.question: Using the lesson's rule of thumb, about how much memory should an 11-billion-parameter model's weights need at 4-bit quantization?
options: About 2 GB, because parameter count is unrelated to memory
About 6.6 GB, from budgeting roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters
About 22 GB, because each parameter always needs two bytes regardless of how it is stored
Exactly 11 GB, because one billion parameters equals one gigabyte
questions.explanation: The lesson's rule of thumb is roughly 0.6 GB of memory per billion parameters at 4-bit. For 11 billion parameters that is about 6.6 GB of weights, before adding context-window and runtime headroom.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what mainly sets the single-stream speed of a locally running model for one user?
options: How fast memory can move the model's weights into the compute units, roughly tokens per second equals memory bandwidth divided by bytes of model
The exact spelling of the prompt, because tokenization dominates all latency
The number of concurrent users, because one user always runs at the same speed no matter the hardware
The network round trip to the model provider, since local models still depend on a hosted API
questions.explanation: For one user, inference is bounded by how quickly the machine can stream weights from memory into the compute units. A smaller quantized model moves fewer bytes per token, which is why it feels faster on the same hardware.
